1 Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “12 2Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When any man3 has a discharge from his body, because of his discharge he is unclean.4✦ 3 This shall be his uncleanness in his discharge: whether his body runs with his discharge, or his body has stopped from his discharge, it is his uncleanness.5✦ 4 “‘Every bed on which he who has the discharge lies shall be unclean; and everything he sits on shall be unclean.6✦ 5 Whoever touches his bed shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water7, and be unclean until the evening.8✦ 6 He who sits on anything on which the man who has the discharge sat shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water9, and be unclean until the evening.10✦ 7 “‘He who touches the body of him who has the discharge shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water11, and be unclean until the evening.12✦ 8 “‘If he who has the discharge spits on him who is clean, then he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water13, and be unclean until the evening.14✦ 9 “‘Whatever saddle he who has the discharge rides on shall be unclean.15✦ 10 Whoever touches anything that was under him shall be unclean until the evening. He who carries those things shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water16, and be unclean until the evening.17✦ 11 “‘Whomever he who has the discharge touches, without having rinsed his hands in water18, he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the evening.19✦ 12 “‘The earth20en vessel, which he who has the discharge touches, shall be broken; and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water21.22✦ 13 “‘When he who has a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count to himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes; and he shall bathe his flesh in running water23, and shall be clean.24✦ 14 “‘On the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, and come before Yahweh to the door of the Tent of Meeting, and give them to the priest.2526✦ 15 The priest shall offer them, the one for a sin27 offering, and the other for a burnt offering. The priest shall make atonement28 for him before Yahweh for his discharge.2930✦ 16 “‘If any man31 has an emission of semen, then he shall bathe all his flesh in water32, and be unclean until the evening.33 17 Every garment and every skin which the semen is on shall be washed with water34, and be unclean until the evening.35 18 If a man36 lies with a woman37 and there is an emission of semen, they shall both bathe themselves in water38, and be unclean until the evening.39 19 “‘If a woman40 has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood41, she shall be in her impurity seven days42. Whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.43 20 “‘Everything that she lies on in her impurity shall be unclean. Everything also that she sits on shall be unclean.44 21 Whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water45, and be unclean until the evening.46 22 Whoever touches anything that she sits on shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water47, and be unclean until the evening.48 23 If it is on the bed, or on anything she sits on, when he touches it, he shall be unclean until the evening.49 24 “‘If any man50 lies with her, and her monthly flow is on him, he shall be unclean seven days; and every bed he lies on shall be unclean.51 25 “‘If a woman52 has a discharge of her blood53 many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period, all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period. She is unclean.54 26 Every bed she lies on all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period. Everything she sits on shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period.55 27 Whoever touches these things shall be unclean, and shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water56, and be unclean until the evening.57 28 “‘But if she is cleansed of her discharge, then she shall count to herself seven days, and after that she shall be clean.58 29 On the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, and bring them to the priest, to the door of the Tent of Meeting.59 30 The priest shall offer the one for a sin60 offering, and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement61 for her before Yahweh for the uncleanness of her discharge.6263✦ 31 “‘Thus you shall separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness64, so they will not die in their uncleanness when they defile my tabernacle that is among them.’”65✦ 32 This is the law of him who has a discharge, and of him who has an emission of semen, so that he is unclean by it;66 33 and of her who has her period, and of a man67 or woman68 who has a discharge, and of him who lies with her who is unclean.

He shall have the linen trousers on his body, and shall put on the linen sash, and he shall be clothed with the linen turban. They are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water11, and put them on.1213✦ 5 He shall take from the congregation of the children of Israel two male goats for a sin14 offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.15✦ 6 “Aaron shall offer the bull of the sin16 offering, which is for himself, and make atonement17 for himself and for his house.18✦ 7 He shall take the two goats, and set them before Yahweh at the door of the Tent of Meeting.1920✦ 8 Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats: one lot for Yahweh, and the other lot for the scapegoat⌘.22232425✦ 9 Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for Yahweh, and offer him for a sin26 offering.2728✦ 10 But the goat on which the lot fell for the scapegoat shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement29 for him, to send him away as the scapegoat into the wilderness.3031✦ 11 “Aaron shall present the bull of the sin32 offering, which is for himself, and shall make atonement33 for himself and for his house, and shall kill the bull of the sin offering which is for himself.34✦ 12 He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from off the altar before Yahweh, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil.3536✦ 13 He shall put the incense on the fire before Yahweh, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy37 seat that is on the covenant, so that he will not die.3839✦ 14 He shall take some of the blood40 of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy41 seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.42✦ 15 “Then he shall kill the goat of the sin43 offering that is for the people, and bring his blood44 within the veil, and do with his blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the mercy45 seat and before the mercy seat.46✦ 16 He shall make atonement47 for the Holy Place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and because of their transgressions, even all their sins; and so he shall do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them in the middle of their uncleanness.4849✦ 17 No one shall be in the Tent of Meeting when he enters to make atonement50 in the Holy Place, until he comes out, and has made atonement for himself and for his household, and for all the assembly of Israel.515253✦ 18 “He shall go out to the altar that is before Yahweh and make atonement54 for it, and shall take some of the bull’s blood55, and some of the goat’s blood, and put it around on the horns of the altar.5657✦ 19 He shall sprinkle some of the blood58 on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it, and make it holy from the uncleanness of the children of Israel.59✦ 20 “When he has finished atoning for the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar, he shall present the live goat.6061✦ 21 Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him62 all the iniquities of the children of Israel63, and all their transgressions, even all their sins; and he shall put them on the head of the goat, and shall send him away into the wilderness by the hand of a man64 who is ready.65✦ 22 The goat shall carry all their iniquities on himself to a solitary land66, and he shall release the goat in the wilderness.67✦ 23 “Aaron shall come into the Tent of Meeting, and shall take off the linen garments which he put on when he went into the Holy Place, and shall leave them there.6869✦ 24 Then he shall bathe himself in water70 in a holy71 place, put on his garments, and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people, and make atonement72 for himself and for the people.73✦ 25 The fat of the sin74 offering he shall burn on the altar.75✦ 26 “He who lets the goat go as the scapegoat shall wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in water76, and afterward he shall come into the camp.77✦ 27 The bull for the sin78 offering, and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood79 was brought in to make atonement80 in the Holy Place, shall be carried outside the camp; and they shall burn their skins, their flesh, and their dung with fire.8182✦ 28 He who burns them shall wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in water83, and afterward he shall come into the camp.84✦ 29 “It shall be a statute to you forever: in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls, and shall do no kind of work, whether native-born or a stranger who lives as a foreigner among you;85✦ 30 for on this day shall atonement86 be made for you, to cleanse you. You shall be clean from all your sins before Yahweh.8788✦ 31 It is a Sabbath of solemn rest to you, and you shall afflict your souls. It is a statute forever.89✦ 32 The priest, who is anointed and who is consecrated to be priest in his father’s place, shall make the atonement90, and shall put on the linen garments, even the holy91 garments.92✦ 33 Then he shall make atonement93 for the Holy Sanctuary; and he shall make atonement for the Tent of Meeting and for the altar; and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly.9495✦ 34 “ This shall be an everlasting statute for you, to make atonement96 for the children of Israel once in the year because of all their sins.” It was done as Yahweh commanded Moses.

12✦1 Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “3 2Speak to Aaron, and to his sons, and to all the children of Israel, and say to them, ‘This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded:4 3 Whatever man5 there is of the house of Israel who kills a bull, or lamb, or goat in the camp, or who kills it outside the camp, 4 and hasn’t brought it to the door of the Tent of Meeting to offer it as an offering to Yahweh before Yahweh’s tabernacle: blood6 shall be imputed to that man7. He has shed blood. That man shall be cut off from among his people.89✦ 5 This is to the end that the children of Israel may bring their sacrifices, which they sacrifice in the open field, that they may bring them to Yahweh, to the door of the Tent of Meeting, to the priest, and sacrifice them for sacrifices of peace10 offerings to Yahweh.11 6 The priest shall sprinkle the blood12 on Yahweh’s altar at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and burn the fat for a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.13 7 They shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to the goat idols, after which they play the prostitute. This shall be a statute forever to them throughout their generations.’14✦ 8 “You shall say to them, ‘Any man15 there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice,16✦ 9 and doesn’t bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting to sacrifice it to Yahweh, that man17 shall be cut off from his people.1819✦ 10 “‘Any man20 of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood21, I will set my face against that soul22 who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people.23✦ 11 For the life of the flesh is in the blood24252627. I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement28 for your soul29s; for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.303132✦ 12 Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person among you may eat blood33, nor may any stranger who lives as a foreigner among you eat blood.”3435✦ 13 “‘Whatever man36 there is of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who takes in hunting any animal or bird that may be eaten, he shall pour out its blood37, and cover it with dust38.39✦ 14 For as to the life of all flesh, its blood40 is with its life. Therefore I said to the children of Israel, “You shall not eat the blood of any kind of flesh; for the life of all flesh is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off.”41✦ 15 “‘Every person that eats what dies of itself, or that which is torn by animals, whether he is native-born or a foreigner, shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water42, and be unclean until the evening. Then he shall be clean.4344✦ 16 But if he doesn’t wash them, or bathe his flesh, then he shall bear his iniquity.’”

You shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, where I am bringing you. You shall not follow their statutes.7✦ 4 You shall do my ordinances. You shall keep my statutes and walk in them. I am Yahweh your God8.9✦ 5 You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances, which if a man10 does, he shall live in them◇. I am Yahweh.12✦ 6 “‘None of you shall approach any close relatives, to uncover their nakedness: I am Yahweh.1314✦ 7 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. It is your father’s nakedness.16 9 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father, or the daughter of your mother, whether born at home or born abroad.17 10 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son’s daughter, or of your daughter’s daughter, even their nakedness; for theirs is your own nakedness.18 11 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, conceived by your father, since she is your sister.19 12 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s sister. She is your father’s near kinswoman.20 13 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother’s sister, for she is your mother’s near kinswoman.21 14 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother. You shall not approach his wife. She is your aunt.22 15 “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law. She is your son’s wife. It is wickedness.26 18 “‘You shall not take a wife in addition to her sister, to be a rival, to uncover her nakedness, while her sister is still alive.27 19 “‘You shall not approach a woman28 to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is impure by her uncleanness.29 20 “‘You shall not lie carnally with your neighbor’s wife, and defile yourself with her.30 21 “‘You shall not give any of your children as a sacrifice to Molech31. You shall not profane the name of your God32. I am Yahweh.3334✦ 22 “‘You shall not lie with a man as with a woman35. That is detestable.363738 23 “‘You shall not lie with any animal to defile yourself with it. Therefore I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out her inhabitants.43✦ 26 You therefore shall keep my statutes and my ordinances, and shall not do any of these abominations; neither the native-born, nor the stranger who lives as a foreigner among you✦ 27 (for the men of the land44 that were before you had done all these abominations, and the land became defiled),45✦ 28 that the land46 not vomit you out also, when you defile it, as it vomited out the nation that was before you.47✦ 29 “‘For whoever shall do any of these abominations, even the souls that do them shall be cut off from among their people.✦ 30 Therefore you shall keep my requirements, that you do not practice any of these abominable customs which were practiced before you, and that you do not defile yourselves with them. I am Yahweh your God48.’”

He shall be holy20 to you, for I Yahweh, who sanctify you, am holy.2122✦ 9 “‘The daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by playing the prostitute, she profanes her father. They will fall when no one pursues.74✦ 37 They will stumble over one another, as it were before the sword, when no one pursues. You will have no power to stand before your enemies.75✦ 38 You will perish among the nations. The land76 of your enemies will eat you up.77✦ 39 Those of you who are left will pine away in their iniquity in your enemies’ lands; and also in the iniquities of their fathers they shall pine away with them.78✦ 40 “‘If they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers, in their trespass which they trespassed against me; and also that because they walked contrary to me,79✦ 41 I also walked contrary to them, and brought them into the land80 of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled, and they then accept the punishment of their iniquity,81✦ 42 then I will remember82 my covenant83 with Jacob, my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham; and I will remember the land84.85✦ 43 The land86 also will be left by them, and will enjoy its Sabbaths while it lies desolate without them; and they will accept the punishment of their iniquity because they rejected my ordinances, and their soul87 abhorred my statutes.88✦ 44 Yet for all that, when they are in the land89 of their enemies, I will not reject them, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly and to break my covenant90 with them; for I am Yahweh their God91.9293 45 But I will for their sake remember the covenant94 of their ancestors, whom I brought out of the land95 of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God96. I am Yahweh.’”9798 46 These are the statutes, ordinances, and laws, which Yahweh made between him and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by Moses.

27

12✦1 Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “3✦ 2Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them, ‘When a man4 consecrates a person to Yahweh in a vow, according to your valuation,56✦ 3 your valuation of a male from twenty years old to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver7, according to the shekel of the sanctuary.8✦ 4 If she is a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels.9✦ 5 If the person is from five years old to twenty years old, then your valuation shall be for a male twenty shekels, and for a female ten shekels.10✦ 6 If the person is from a month old to five years old, then your valuation shall be for a male five shekels of silver, and for a female your valuation shall be three shekels of silver.11✦ 7 If the person is from sixty years old and upward; if he is a male, then your valuation shall be fifteen shekels, and for a female ten shekels.12✦ 8 But if he is poorer than your valuation, then he shall be set before the priest, and the priest shall assign a value to him. The priest shall assign a value according to his ability to pay.13✦ 9 “‘If it is an animal of which men offer an offering to Yahweh, all that any man14 gives of such to Yahweh becomes holy15.1617✦ 10 He shall not alter it, nor exchange it, a good18 for a bad, or a bad for a good. If he shall at all exchange animal for animal, then both it and that for which it is exchanged shall be holy19.20✦ 11 If it is any unclean animal, of which they do not offer as an offering to Yahweh, then he shall set the animal before the priest;2122✦ 12 and the priest shall evaluate it, whether it is good23 or bad. As the priest evaluates it, so it shall be.24✦ 13 But if he will indeed redeem25 it, then he shall add the fifth part of it to its valuation.26✦ 14 “‘When a man27 dedicates his house to be holy28 to Yahweh, then the priest shall evaluate it, whether it is good29 or bad. As the priest evaluates it, so it shall stand.3031✦ 15 If he who dedicates it will redeem32 his house, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall be his.33✦ 16 “‘If a man34 dedicates to Yahweh part of the field of his possession, then your valuation shall be according to the seed for it. The sowing of a homer of barley shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver.353637✦ 17 If he dedicates his field from the Year of Jubilee, according to your valuation it shall stand.38✦ 18 But if he dedicates his field after the Jubilee, then the priest shall reckon to him the money according to the years that remain to the Year of Jubilee; and an abatement shall be made from your valuation.39✦ 19 If he who dedicated the field will indeed redeem40 it, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall remain his.41✦ 20 If he will not redeem42 the field, or if he has sold the field to another man43, it shall not be redeemed any more;44✦ 21 but the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee, shall be holy45 to Yahweh, as a devoted field. It shall be owned by the priests.4647✦ 22 “‘If he dedicates a field to Yahweh which he has bought, which is not of the field of his possession,484950✦ 23 then the priest shall reckon to him the worth of your valuation up to the Year of Jubilee; and he shall give your valuation on that day, as a holy51 thing to Yahweh.5253✦ 24 In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, even to him to whom the possession of the land54 belongs.55✦ 25 All your valuations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs to the shekel.5657✦ 26 “‘However the firstborn among animals, which belongs to Yahweh as a firstborn, no man58 may dedicate, whether an ox or a sheep. It is Yahweh’s.5960✦ 27 If it is an unclean animal, then he shall buy it back according to your valuation, and shall add to it the fifth part of it; or if it isn’t redeem61ed, then it shall be sold according to your valuation.62✦ 28 “‘Notwithstanding, no devoted thing that a man63 devotes to Yahweh of all that he has, whether of man or animal, or of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed. Everything that is permanently devoted is most holy64 to Yahweh.6566✦ 29 “‘No one devoted to destruction, who shall be devoted from among men, shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death.67✦ 30 “‘All the tithe of the land6869, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy70 to Yahweh.7172✦ 31 If a man73 redeem74s anything of his tithe, he shall add a fifth part to it.75✦ 32 All the tithe of the herds or the flocks, whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy76 to Yahweh.7778✦ 33 He shall not examine whether it is good79 or bad, neither shall he exchange it. If he exchanges it at all, then both it and that for which it is exchanged shall be holy80. It shall not be redeemed.’”81✦ 34 These are the commandments which Yahweh commanded Moses for the children of Israel on Mount Sinai.82✦

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). COAT the tunic worn like the shirt next the skin (Leviticus 16:4; Cant. 5:3; 2 Samuel 15:32; Exodus 28:4; 29:5). The “coats of skins” prepared by God for Adam and Eve were probably nothing more than aprons (Genesis 3:21). This tunic was sometimes woven entire without a seam (John 19:23); it was also sometimes of “many colours” (Genesis 37:3; R.V. marg., “a long garment with sleeves”). The “fisher’s coat” of John 21:7 was obviously an outer garment or cloak, as was also the “coat” made by Hannah for Samuel (1 Samuel 2:19). (See DRESS.)

↩ ⌘ Hebrew Azazel (עֲזָאזֵל). One of the most disputed words in the entire Hebrew Bible. Four major readings: (1) a wilderness demon to whom the goat is dispatched (the reading favored by 1 Enoch 10 and most modern scholars); (2) a place name, “rugged cliff,” where the goat is led (rabbinic tradition); (3) a compound noun, ‘ez ozel, “the goat that goes away” (whence Tyndale’s English coinage scapegoat, 1530); (4) a contraction of an older Canaanite divine name. The translation choice silently commits the reader to one of these.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ʼădônây (אֲדֹנָי). the Lord (used as a proper name of God only).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). AZAZEL (Leviticus 16:8, 10, 26, Revised Version only here; rendered “scape-goat” in the Authorized Version). This word has given rise to many different views. Some Jewish interpreters regard it as the name of a place some 12 miles east of Jerusalem, in the wilderness. Others take it to be the name of an evil spirit, or even of Satan. But when we remember that the two goats together form a type of Christ, on whom the Lord “laid the iniquity of us all,” and examine into the root meaning of this word (viz., “separation”), the interpretation of those who regard the one goat as representing the atonement made, and the other, that “for Azazel,” as representing the effect of the great work of atonement (viz., the complete removal of sin), is certainly to be preferred. The one goat which was “for Jehovah” was offered as a sin-offering, by which atonement was made. But the sins must also be visibly banished, and therefore they were symbolically laid by confession on the other goat, which was then “sent away for Azazel” into the wilderness. The form of this word indicates intensity, and therefore signifies the total separation of sin: it was wholly carried away. It was important that the result of the sacrifices offered by the high priest alone in the sanctuary should be embodied in a visible transaction, and hence the dismissal of the “scape-goat.” It was of no consequence what became of it, as the whole import of the transaction lay in its being sent into the wilderness bearing away sin. As the goat “for Jehovah” was to witness to the demerit of sin and the need of the blood of atonement, so the goat “for Azazel” was to witness to the efficacy of the sacrifice and the result of the shedding of blood in the taking away of sin.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SCAPEGOAT Leviticus 16:8-26; R.V., “the goat for Azazel” (q.v.), the name given to the goat which was taken away into the wilderness on the day of Atonement (16:20-22). The priest made atonement over the scapegoat, laying Israel’s guilt upon it, and then sent it away, the goat bearing “upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited.” At a later period an evasion or modification of the law of Moses was introduced by the Jews. “The goat was conducted to a mountain named Tzuk, situated at a distance of ten Sabbath days’ journey, or about six and a half English miles, from Jerusalem. At this place the Judean desert was supposed to commence; and the man in whose charge the goat was sent out, while setting him free, was instructed to push the unhappy beast down the slope of the mountain side, which was so steep as to insure the death of the goat, whose bones were broken by the fall. The reason of this barbarous custom was that on one occasion the scapegoat returned to Jerusalem after being set free, which was considered such an evil omen that its recurrence was prevented for the future by the death of the goat” (Twenty-one Years’ Work in the Holy Land). This mountain is now called el-Muntar.

↩ ◇ Note. The transfer of sin. The high priest verbally enumerates Israel’s sins while pressing both hands on the goat. Two animals are required (16:5): one is sacrificed “for YHWH,” the other sent live to the wilderness. The pair functions as a single rite — purification of the sanctuary plus removal of the polluting sin from the community. The English term scapegoat for an innocent who carries another’s blame derives directly from this passage.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Nephesh ha-basar ba-dam (נֶפֶשׁ הַבָּשָׂר בַּדָּם). The verse equates nephesh (often “soul,” here closer to “life-force”) with blood. From this emerges the universal Israelite blood-prohibition: blood belongs to God because life belongs to God. The rationale shows that Israelite sacrifice is not transactional payment but an exchange of life-essences. The verse becomes the theological core text for many later interpretations of atonement, including the New Testament’s reading of the death of Jesus.

↩ ◇ Note Live by them. The verse becomes a key New Testament proof-text in the law/grace debate. Paul cites it in Gal 3:12 and Rom 10:5 as expressing the "do this and live" logic of law-righteousness, contrasted with faith-righteousness. The rabbinic reading runs the opposite way: "live by them, and not die by them" (b. Yoma 85b) — the foundational rabbinic principle of piku‘aḥ nefesh, that almost any commandment may be set aside to save a life.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GLEAN The corners of fields were not to be reaped, and the sheaf accidentally left behind was not to be fetched away, according to the law of Moses (Leviticus 19:9; 23:22; Deuteronomy 24:21). They were to be left for the poor to glean. Similar laws were given regarding vineyards and oliveyards. (Comp. Ruth 2:2.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). POOR The Mosaic legislation regarding the poor is specially important. (1.) They had the right of gleaning the fields (Leviticus 19:9, 10; Deuteronomy 24:19,21). (2.) In the sabbatical year they were to have their share of the produce of the fields and the vineyards (Exodus 23:11; Leviticus 25:6). (3.) In the year of jubilee they recovered their property (Leviticus 25:25-30). (4.) Usury was forbidden, and the pledged raiment was to be returned before the sun went down (Exodus 22:25-27; Deuteronomy 24:10-13). The rich were to be generous to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7-11). (5.) In the sabbatical and jubilee years the bond-servant was to go free (Deuteronomy 15:12-15; Leviticus 25:39-42, 47-54). (6.) Certain portions from the tithes were assigned to the poor (Deuteronomy 14:28, 29; 26:12, 13). (7.) They shared in the feasts (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14; Nehemiah 8:10). (8.) Wages were to be paid at the close of each day (Leviticus 19:13). In the New Testament (Luke 3:11; 14:13; Acts 6:1; Galatians 2:10; James 2:15, 16) we have similar injunctions given with reference to the poor. Begging was not common under the Old Testament, while it was so in the New Testament times (Luke 16:20, 21, etc.). But begging in the case of those who are able to work is forbidden, and all such are enjoined to “work with their own hands” as a Christian duty (1 Thessalonians 4:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:7-13; Ephesians 4:28). This word is used figuratively in Matthew 5:3; Luke 6:20; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Revelation 3:17.

↩ ◇ Note. The Golden Rule’s scriptural source. Both Hillel and Jesus identify this verse (or its negative form) as the summary of the Torah (b. Shabbat 31a, Mark 12:31). The Hebrew re‘akha kamokha can also be read as “your neighbor [who is] like yourself” — i.e. love them because they share your humanity. The original scope of re’a is the fellow Israelite; verse 34 of the same chapter explicitly extends the love-command to the resident foreigner.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Kil’ayim (כִּלְאַיִם) — forbidden mixtures. Three are listed: cross-breeding livestock, sowing two seeds in one field, wearing wool-and-linen (shaatnez) cloth. The unifying logic is that creation’s ordained categories should not be blurred — the same logic underlies the food laws of chapter 11. Shaatnez remains observed in Orthodox Jewish practice today; garments are tested for forbidden fibre combinations.

↩ ◇ Note. The most contested verse in modern Leviticus interpretation. Hebrew: v’ish asher yishkav et zakhar mishk’vei ishah. Readings range across a wide field, including the traditional view that all male same-sex relations are forbidden; readings that limit the scope to particular contexts (e.g. cult prostitution, exploitation, or one specific role); and readings that focus on the rare phrase mishk’vei ishah (“the lyings of a woman”). The interpretive debate is genuinely live in scholarship and religious communities. The corresponding female case is not addressed here.

↩ ◇ Note The holiness of the Name. The verse establishes the principle of kiddush ha-Shem ("sanctification of the Name") — and its negative counterpart chillul ha-Shem ("desecration of the Name") — that runs through the rest of OT and Jewish theology. Ezekiel’s long meditation on Yahweh’s reputation among the nations (Ezek 36:20–23) draws directly on this principle: Israel’s exile has profaned the divine name, and Yahweh will restore Israel for his name’s sake. The Lord’s Prayer’s opening petition ("hallowed be your name," Matt 6:9) is built on the same theological foundation. In rabbinic Judaism, kiddush ha-Shem becomes the framework for martyrdom theology: dying rather than violating Torah is the highest form of sanctifying the Name (b. Sanhedrin 74a). The verse is one of the OT’s most consequential single sentences, generating two and a half millennia of Jewish ethical-theological reflection on the relationship between divine reputation and Israelite conduct.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CONVOCATION a meeting of a religious character as distinguished from congregation, which was more general, dealing with political and legal matters. Hence it is called an “holy convocation.” Such convocations were the Sabbaths (Leviticus 23:2, 3), the Passover (Exodus 12:16; Leviticus 23:7, 8; Numbers 28:25), Pentecost (Leviticus 23:21), the feast of Trumpets (Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 29:1), the feast of Weeks (Numbers 28:26), and the feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:35, 36). The great fast, the annual day of atonement, was “the holy convocation” (Leviticus 23:27; Numbers 29:7).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FIRST-FRUITS The first-fruits of the ground were offered unto God just as the first-born of man and animals. The law required, (1.) That on the morrow after the Passover Sabbath a sheaf of new corn should be waved by the priest before the altar (Leviticus 23:5, 6, 10, 12; 2:12). (2.) That at the feast of Pentecost two loaves of leavened bread, made from the new flour, were to be waved in like manner (Leviticus 23:15, 17; Numbers 28:26). (3.) The feast of Tabernacles was an acknowledgement that the fruits of the harvest were from the Lord (Exodus 23:16; 34:22). (4.) Every individual, besides, was required to consecrate to God a portion of the first-fruits of the land (Exodus 22:29; 23:19; 34:26; Numbers 15:20, 21). (5.) The law enjoined that no fruit was to be gathered from newly-planted fruit-trees for the first three years, and that the first-fruits of the fourth year were to be consecrated to the Lord (Leviticus 19:23-25). Jeremiah (2:3) alludes to the ordinance of “first-fruits,” and hence he must have been acquainted with the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, where the laws regarding it are recorded.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HARVEST the season for gathering grain or fruit. On the 16th day of Abib (or April) a handful of ripe ears of corn was offered as a first-fruit before the Lord, and immediately after this the harvest commenced (Leviticus 23:9-14; 2 Samuel 21:9, 10; Ruth 2:23). It began with the feast of Passover and ended with Pentecost, thus lasting for seven weeks (Exodus 23:16). The harvest was a season of joy (Psalm 126:1-6; Isaiah 9:3). This word is used figuratively Matthew 9:37; 13:30; Luke 10:2; John 4:35. (See AGRICULTURE.)

↩ ◇ Note Counting the Omer. The seven-week count from the second day of Passover to Shavuot (Pentecost). Still observed daily in Jewish liturgy. The festival on the fiftieth day, originally an agricultural first-fruits feast, became in rabbinic tradition the celebration of the giving of the Torah at Sinai. In the New Testament, the same fiftieth day becomes Pentecost (Acts 2) — the giving of the Spirit. The structural parallel between Torah-giving and Spirit-giving on the same calendar day is foundational to early Christian theology.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TRUMPETS , FEAST OF was celebrated at the beginning of the month Tisri, the first month of the civil year. It received its name from the circumstances that the trumpets usually blown at the commencement of each month were on that occasion blown with unusual solemnity (Leviticus 23:23-25; Numbers 10:10; 29:1-6). It was one of the seven days of holy convocation. The special design of this feast, which is described in these verses, is not known.

↩ ◇ Note The festival that became Rosh Hashanah. The Torah names the first day of the seventh month only as zikhron teru‘ah (“memorial of blasts”) — there is no explicit “New Year” language, since biblical Israel reckoned the new year from spring (Nisan). The shift to a fall new year is post-biblical; Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 ultimately recognizes four distinct new-years for different purposes.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SABBATICAL YEAR every seventh year, during which the land, according to the law of Moses, had to remain uncultivated (Leviticus 25:2-7; comp. Exodus 23:10, 11, 12; Leviticus 26:34, 35). Whatever grew of itself during that year was not for the owner of the land, but for the poor and the stranger and the beasts of the field. All debts, except those of foreigners, were to be remitted (Deuteronomy 15:1-11). There is little notice of the observance of this year in Biblical history. It appears to have been much neglected (2 Chronicles 36:20, 21).

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Dror (דְּרוֹר) — “release.” Cognate with Akkadian andurāru, a royal proclamation cancelling debts and freeing certain classes of slaves at the start of a new king’s reign. Israel domesticates an established Mesopotamian institution and makes it routine — every fiftieth year, by divine decree, not royal whim. The verse is inscribed on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JUBILEE a joyful shout or clangour of trumpets, the name of the great semi-centennial festival of the Hebrews. It lasted for a year. During this year the land was to be fallow, and the Israelites were only permitted to gather the spontaneous produce of the fields (Leviticus 25:11, 12). All landed property during that year reverted to its original owner (13-34; 27:16-24), and all who were slaves were set free (25:39-54), and all debts were remitted. The return of the jubilee year was proclaimed by a blast of trumpets which sounded throughout the land. There is no record in Scripture of the actual observance of this festival, but there are numerous allusions (Isaiah 5:7, 8, 9, 10; 61:1, 2; Ezekiel 7:12, 13; Nehemiah 5:1-19; 2 Chronicles 36:21) which place it beyond a doubt that it was observed. The advantages of this institution were manifold. “1. It would prevent the accumulation of land on the part of a few to the detriment of the community at large. 2. It would render it impossible for any one to be born to absolute poverty, since every one had his hereditary land. 3. It would preclude those inequalities which are produced by extremes of riches and poverty, and which make one man domineer over another. 4. It would utterly do away with slavery. 5. It would afford a fresh opportunity to those who were reduced by adverse circumstances to begin again their career of industry in the patrimony which they had temporarily forfeited. 6. It would periodically rectify the disorders which crept into the state in the course of time, preclude the division of the people into nobles and plebeians, and preserve the theocracy inviolate.”

↩ ◇ Note. Land theology. The Jubilee laws presuppose that Israel does not own the land — God does. Every household holds an inheritance from God, never as absolute property. Land sales between Israelites are technically leases until the next jubilee. This theological framework underlies prophetic critiques of land accumulation (Isaiah 5:8, Micah 2:1–2) and shapes much of the Hebrew Bible’s political economy.

The verb form hithpa‘el of halakh (“to walk”) is the same form used of God in Eden (Gen 3:8) — an iterative, easy walking-about. The covenantal blessing is framed as a return to Edenic intimacy: God resumes walking in the midst of his people as he once walked in the garden. Paul cites this verse in 2 Corinthians 6:16.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant curses. Verses 14–39 follow the form of an ancient Near Eastern suzerain-vassal treaty: blessings for fidelity, curses for breach. Comparable lists appear in Hittite treaties of the second millennium BCE. The Israelite version is distinctive in two ways: the curses are escalating (each round if-they-still-don’t-listen — verses 18, 21, 23, 27), and the chapter ends not in destruction but in the possibility of confession and restoration (40–45).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JORDAN Hebrews Yarden, “the descender;” Arab. Nahr-esh-Sheriah, “the watering-place” the chief river of Palestine. It flows from north to south down a deep valley in the centre of the country. The name descender is significant of the fact that there is along its whole course a descent to its banks; or it may simply denote the rapidity with which it “descends” to the Dead Sea. It originates in the snows of Hermon, which feed its perennial fountains. Two sources are generally spoken of. (1.) From the western base of a hill on which once stood the city of Dan, the northern border-city of Palestine, there gushes forth a considerable fountain called the Leddan, which is the largest fountain in Syria and the principal source of the Jordan. (2.) Beside the ruins of Banias, the ancient Caesarea Philippi and the yet more ancient Panium, is a lofty cliff of limestone, at the base of which is a fountain. This is the other source of the Jordan, and has always been regarded by the Jews as its true source. It rushes down to the plain in a foaming torrent, and joins the Leddan about 5 miles south of Dan (Tell-el-Kady). (3.) But besides these two historical fountains there is a third, called the Hasbany, which rises in the bottom of a valley at the western base of Hermon, 12 miles north of Tell-el-Kady. It joins the main stream about a mile below the junction of the Leddan and the Banias. The river thus formed is at this point about 45 feet wide, and flows in a channel from 12 to 20 feet below the plain. After this it flows, “with a swift current and a much-twisted course,” through a marshy plain for some 6 miles, when it falls into the Lake Huleh, “the waters of Merom” (q.v.). During this part of its course the Jordan has descended about 1,100 feet. At Banias it is 1,080 feet above sea-level. Flowing from the southern extremity of Lake Huleh, here almost on a level with the sea, it flows for 2 miles “through a waste of islets and papyrus,” and then for 9 miles through a narrow gorge in a foaming torrent onward to the Sea of Galilee (q.v.). “In the whole valley of the Jordan from the Lake Huleh to the Sea of Galilee there is not a single settled inhabitant. Along the whole eastern bank of the river and the lakes, from the base of Hermon to the ravine of Hieromax, a region of great fertility, 30 miles long by 7 or 8 wide, there are only some three inhabited villages. The western bank is almost as desolate. Ruins are numerous enough. Every mile or two is an old site of town or village, now well nigh hid beneath a dense jungle of thorns and thistles. The words of Scripture here recur to us with peculiar force: ‘I will make your cities waste, and bring your sanctuaries unto desolation...And I will bring the land into desolation: and your enemies which dwell therein shall be astonished at it...And your land shall be desolate, and your cities waste. Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths, as long as it lieth desolate’ (Leviticus 26:31-34).”, Dr. Porter’s Handbook. From the Sea of Galilee, at the level of 682 feet below the Mediterranean, the river flows through a long, low plain called “the region of Jordan” (Matthew 3:5), and by the modern Arabs the Ghor, or “sunken plain.” This section is properly the Jordan of Scripture. Down through the midst of the “plain of Jordan” there winds a ravine varying in breadth from 200 yards to half a mile, and in depth from 40 to 150 feet. Through it the Jordan flows in a rapid, rugged, tortuous course down to the Dead Sea. The whole distance from the southern extremity of the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea is in a straight line about 65 miles, but following the windings of the river about 200 miles, during which it falls 618 feet. The total length of the Jordan from Banias is about 104 miles in a straight line, during which it falls 2,380 feet. There are two considerable affluents which enter the river between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea, both from the east. (1.) The Wady Mandhur, called the Yarmuk by the Rabbins and the Hieromax by the Greeks. It formed the boundary between Bashan and Gilead. It drains the plateau of the Hauran. (2.) The Jabbok or Wady Zerka, formerly the northern boundary of Ammon. It enters the Jordan about 20 miles north of Jericho. The first historical notice of the Jordan is in the account of the separation of Abraham and Lot (Genesis 13:10). “Lot beheld the plain of Jordan as the garden of the Lord.” Jacob crossed and recrossed “this Jordan” (32:10). The Israelites passed over it as “on dry ground” (Joshua 3:17; Psalm 114:3). Twice afterwards its waters were miraculously divided at the same spot by Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:8, 14). The Jordan is mentioned in the Old Testament about one hundred and eighty times, and in the New Testament fifteen times. The chief events in gospel history connected with it are (1) John the Baptist’s ministry, when “there went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and were baptized of him in Jordan” (Matthew 3:6). (2.) Jesus also “was baptized of John in Jordan” (Mark 1:9).

↩ ◇ Note. The gleaning laws. One of the earliest legislated welfare provisions in the ancient Near East. The corners (pe’ah) and the gleanings (leqet) belong by right to the poor and the foreigner — not as charity but as their portion of the harvest. The book of Ruth turns on this institution (Ruth 2:2–3). Modern Jewish practice retains pe’ah as a category, often translated into financial giving where the original agricultural form is impractical.

↩ ◇ Note. Molech. A Canaanite/Phoenician deity associated with child sacrifice. The Tophet at Carthage (a Phoenician colony) has yielded thousands of cremation urns containing infant remains, providing physical evidence that such sacrifices were practiced. The Hebrew Bible’s denunciations of Molech worship (Lev 18:21, 20:2–5; 2 Kgs 23:10; Jer 7:31, 32:35) are not polemical fiction but reflect a real religious option in the ancient Near East that Israel’s legislation flatly prohibited. The location at Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom (Gei Hinnom) eventually generated the New Testament word gehenna.

↩ ◇ Note. Priestly purity. The priestly class is held to a higher purity standard than ordinary Israelites: no contact with corpses except for the closest relatives (21:2–3), no marriage to divorced women (21:7), no bodily blemishes for the high priest (21:17–23). The rules are not moral but cultic-symbolic — the priesthood embodies the principle of wholeness that the sanctuary itself instantiates. Many of these provisions were carried over and adapted in early Christian and especially Eastern Orthodox clerical discipline.

↩ ◇ Note. The Jubilee year. The fiftieth year of the cycle — slaves freed, debts forgiven, alienated land returned to original families (25:10). Jesus quotes Isa 61, which is itself a Jubilee text, in his Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:18–19). Whether Jubilee was ever consistently practiced historically is debated by scholars — the prophetic literature laments its non-observance (Jer 34). The Liberty Bell in Philadelphia bears the inscription from 25:10 ("proclaim liberty throughout the land"), one of the most-quoted Pentateuchal verses in American civic memory.

↩ ◇ Note. The scapegoat. The high priest verbally transfers Israel’s sins onto the second goat, which is then driven into the wilderness to Azazel. This is the only place in scripture where sins are verbally rather than ritually transferred. The English word "scapegoat" (Tyndale, 1530) was coined from this very verse. Hebrews 9 reads the entire Day of Atonement liturgy Christologically: Jesus as both sacrificed goat and high priest, entering the heavenly sanctuary once for all.

↩ ◇ Note. Blood as life. The verse grounds the kosher prohibition on consuming blood and the ritual centrality of blood in atonement. "The blood that makes atonement by reason of the life" — life-for-life, the soul-substitution principle. Hebrews 9:22 ("without shedding of blood is no remission") is a direct citation. The priestly conception of life (nefesh) as fluid and continuous with breath is part of the Hebrew Bible’s distinctive anthropology.

↩ ◇ Note. The second great commandment. Jesus pairs this with Deut 6:4–5 (Mark 12:28–34) as the summary of the law. Rabbi Akiva called it "the great principle of the Torah." Hillel rendered it negatively ("what is hateful to you, do not do to another"). The verse’s placement matters: it follows three commandments about not-mistreating-others (vv.16–17), and in v.34 the same standard is extended to the resident foreigner. The "as yourself" comparison assumes a baseline of legitimate self-regard.

↩ ◇ Note. Yom Teru‘ah / Rosh Hashanah. Leviticus calls it "a memorial of blast of trumpets" — only later does it become Rosh Hashanah, the New Year. The shofar’s blast is read in Jewish tradition as a wake-up to repentance, the announcement of the divine King, a memorial of the binding of Isaac (the ram caught in the thicket), and the proclamation of the messianic redemption. The Ethiopian Tewahedo liturgical year preserves an analogous trumpet motif at Mäskäräm.

↩ ◇ Note. The Jubilee. Every fiftieth year, debts canceled, slaves freed, ancestral lands returned. The economic radicalism of the Jubilee — a built-in reset of inequality — has shaped Jewish, Christian, and modern social thought. The phrase "proclaim liberty throughout the land" from this passage is engraved on the Liberty Bell (Philadelphia). Scholars debate whether the Jubilee was historically practiced or remained an ideal. Jesus invokes it at Luke 4:18–19, citing Isa 61, where the "acceptable year of the Lord" is the Jubilee.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant blessing. The verb halakh ("walk") echoes Eden — God walking in the garden in the cool of the day (Gen 3:8). The blessing-curse structure of Lev 26 (parallel to Deut 28) frames the whole covenant: blessing for fidelity, curse for infidelity, but with a hinge of restoration at the end (vv.40–45). Paul cites a piece of this verse in 2 Cor 6:16 ("I will dwell in them") to apply the covenant promise to the church.

↩ ◇ Note. The menstruation laws. The chapter places menstrual impurity within the same category as bodily-discharge impurities (15:1–18 covers male discharges; 15:19–24 menstrual; 15:25–30 abnormal female discharges). The seven-day impurity period for menstruation, plus the secondary impurity of objects she sits or lies on, organizes household life around the menstrual cycle in significant ways. The chapter is the textual root of the Jewish niddah tradition and its mikveh-bath of post-menstrual purification. Modern feminist OT scholarship has read the chapter from multiple angles — Phyllis Trible, Tikva Frymer-Kensky, and Jacob Milgrom each emphasize different aspects: the symmetric treatment of male and female bodily impurities (against the older view that the chapter targeted women specifically), the genuine social regulation of intimate space, and the chapter’s eventual transformation in rabbinic Judaism into a system that women themselves maintained as religiously meaningful. The verse continues to generate substantial scholarly and devotional discussion.

↩ ◇ Note. The chapter’s theological hinge. The verse provides the framing principle for the entire purity-system the chapter has just laid out: separation from uncleanness is not just hygiene or social regulation but specifically protection from defiling Yahweh’s tabernacle. The cult is the focal point at which impurity becomes deadly — "so they will not die in their uncleanness when they defile my tabernacle." The chapter’s logic is concentric: ordinary household impurity is manageable; the same impurity entering sacred space generates lethal consequence. Mary Douglas’s Purity and Danger (1966) made this chapter one of the foundational texts of modern anthropological-theological reflection on impurity systems. Christian theological appropriation has often dismissed the purity laws as superseded by the gospel; modern OT scholarship has tended to recover them as a coherent theology of holiness-by-distance, where ordinary life is sustained partly by maintaining buffers between everyday impurity and the cultic center. The verse encodes the principle the entire chapter has been illustrating.

↩ ◇ Note. Blood, life, atonement. One of the most theologically charged verses in the Pentateuch. The verse links three things: blood = life (nefesh), life given on the altar effects atonement, the prohibition on consuming blood follows from blood’s sacral function. Hebrews 9:22 cites this principle ("without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness"). The verse underwrites both Jewish ritual slaughter (shechita, which drains blood) and the Christian theology of the cross.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ALIEN a foreigner, or person born in another country, and therefore not entitled to the rights and privileges of the country where he resides. Among the Hebrews there were two classes of aliens. (1.) Those who were strangers generally, and who owned no landed property. (2.) Strangers dwelling in another country without being naturalized (Leviticus 22:10; Psalm 39:12). Both of these classes were to enjoy, under certain conditions, the same rights as other citizens (Leviticus 19:33, 34; Deuteronomy 10:19). They might be naturalized and permitted to enter into the congregation of the Lord by submitting to circumcision and abandoning idolatry (Deuteronomy 23:3-8). This term is used (Ephesians 2:12) to denote persons who have no interest in Christ.

↩ ◇ Note. The unblemished principle. The chapter requires that all peace-offerings be physically perfect — no blindness, fracture, mutilation, sores, scabs, or scars (22:22). The Hebrew tamim ("perfect, complete, unblemished") is the same term Noah is described by (Gen 6:9, "perfect in his generations") and the same term Christ is described by in 1 Pet 1:19 ("a lamb without blemish or defect"). The Christological appropriation of the unblemished-offering principle is one of the most sustained NT readings of OT cult — the Levitical requirement of physical perfection in the offering becomes the typological ground for the moral perfection of Christ as the one true offering. The OT provision also functions practically: an Israelite tempted to dispose of a defective animal by offering it at the sanctuary (rather than slaughter at home) is forbidden the option, preserving the integrity of cultic substance. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest demonstrations that ritual procedure and moral substance are not separable.

↩ ◇ Note. The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves of fine flour, set on the golden table inside the holy place, replaced weekly by fresh bread, with the old loaves eaten by the priests in a holy place (24:8–9). The number twelve corresponds to the tribes; the weekly replacement maintains the offering as continuously present. David and his men eat this bread at Nob (1 Sam 21:1–6), an episode Jesus cites in defense of his disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath (Mark 2:25–26, Matt 12:3–4, Luke 6:3–4) — the showbread becomes Jesus’ paradigm-text for ritual law yielding to human need. The Hebrew leḥem ha-panim ("bread of the Presence") frames the bread as Yahweh’s table-fellowship with Israel — a perpetual visible sign of divine presence. The Christian Eucharistic tradition draws extensively on this OT institution: the perpetual reservation of the consecrated bread, the table-presence theology, the priestly consumption all have OT antecedents in the showbread procedure.

↩ ◇ Note. The blasphemer’s execution. The chapter records the OT’s only narrative of capital punishment for blasphemy — and the procedure it institutes (the witnesses lay hands on the offender’s head before execution) becomes the standard Israelite procedure for capital cases. The hand-laying gesture is theologically charged: the witnesses transfer responsibility for the death from the community generally to themselves specifically. The same gesture appears in priestly ordination (Lev 8:14), in Joshua’s commissioning by Moses (Num 27:18), and in Christian sacramental ordination across the centuries — the gesture transmits authority and obligation simultaneously. The blasphemer’s execution also illustrates one of the OT’s most-discussed legal principles: the same law applies to native Israelite and resident alien (24:16, 22). The provision is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of equal application of capital law regardless of ethnic identity, an unusual position in ANE legal contexts where most law-codes had distinct procedures for the various social classes.

↩ ◇ Note. The valuation table. The chapter codifies a sliding-scale valuation system for persons dedicated to Yahweh: adult men 50 shekels, adult women 30, boys 20, girls 10, etc. (27:3–7). The differential valuation has generated significant ethical discussion — modern readers often experience it as discriminatory pricing of human worth. Rabbinic and modern critical scholarship offer multiple readings: the values may reflect typical economic productivity in ancient Israelite agricultural-pastoral economies (men producing more market value than women) without implying intrinsic worth distinctions; or they may encode patriarchal valuation that the chapter takes for granted; or they may function as a graduated pricing system to make vow-redemption affordable across different household economies. The chapter ends Leviticus with a note about how vows of persons are to be redeemed financially rather than literally enforced — the final word of the book is a procedural mercy, allowing rash dedications to be commuted to silver. The structural placement matters: Leviticus closes by limiting the binding force of religious enthusiasm.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WEIGHTS Reduced to English troy-weight, the Hebrew weights were: (1.) The gerah (Leviticus 27:25; Numbers 3:47), a Hebrew word, meaning a grain or kernel, and hence a small weight. It was the twentieth part of a shekel, and equal to 12 grains. (2.) Bekah (Exodus 38:26), meaning “a half” i.e., “half a shekel,” equal to 5 pennyweight. (3.) Shekel, “a weight,” only in the Old Testament, and frequently in its original form (Genesis 23:15, 16; Exodus 21:32; 30:13, 15; 38:24-29, etc.). It was equal to 10 pennyweight. (4.) Ma’neh, “a part” or “portion” (Ezekiel 45:12), equal to 60 shekels, i.e., to 2 lbs. 6 oz. (5.) Talent of silver (2 Kings 5:22), equal to 3,000 shekels, i.e., 125 lbs. (6.) Talent of gold (Exodus 25:39), double the preceding, i.e., 250 lbs.

↩ ◇ Note. The tithe principle. The chapter institutes the basic tithe — one-tenth of agricultural produce belonging to Yahweh — that becomes one of the OT’s most enduring cultic-economic obligations. The provision interlocks with several others: the priestly portion (Num 18:21–28), the triennial tithe for the poor (Deut 14:28–29), and Jacob’s pre-legal vow of tithing (Gen 28:22). By the Second Temple period, tithing had become one of the most-discussed legal-religious topics; Jesus’ critique that the Pharisees "tithe mint and dill and cumin and have neglected the weightier matters of the law" (Matt 23:23) reflects the technical elaboration the practice had received. Christian tradition has continued to treat tithing as theologically meaningful, though usually with debate over whether it remains literally binding. The verse is the textual root of one of the most economically and pastorally consequential OT institutions, with effects running into the modern church.

↩ ◇ Note. The verse and its interpretation. The verse — paired with the capital-penalty version at 20:13 — is one of the most contested texts in modern biblical interpretation. Several distinct interpretive traditions exist: traditional readings (rabbinic, patristic, and most Reformation-era and contemporary conservative Christian) take the verse as a categorical prohibition of male same-sex intercourse; some modern revisionist readings (so John Boswell, Robert Gagnon’s opponents in detail) argue the verse targets specific cultic-prostitution practices, exploitative or coercive acts, or pederasty rather than mutual consensual relationships; other modern readers (so Walter Wink) acknowledge the literal prohibition but treat it as part of the OT purity-code that the New Testament’s explicit suspension of the food-and-purity laws (Acts 10–11, 15) substantially reframes; and there is a long tradition of LGBTQ Jewish and Christian readers who have engaged the text from within their own communities of interpretation. The chapter’s placement of this prohibition among a list including incest (18:6–18), child sacrifice (18:21), bestiality (18:23), and adultery (18:20) frames the categorization the original editor intended. Few verses in the OT have generated more sustained scholarly, ecclesial, and personal debate, and the careful interpreter holds the literal sense of the verse together with the long range of interpretive engagement it has produced.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FORNICATION in every form of it was sternly condemned by the Mosaic law (Leviticus 21:9; 19:29; Deuteronomy 22:20, 21, 23-29; 23:18; Exodus 22:16). (See ADULTERY.) But this word is more frequently used in a symbolical than in its ordinary sense. It frequently means a forsaking of God or a following after idols (Isaiah 1:2; Jeremiah 2:20; Ezekiel 16; Hos. 1:2; 2:1-5; Jeremiah 3:8,9).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: High Priest, The.

↩ ◇ Note. The high priest’s restrictions. The chapter lays unusually stringent purity restrictions on the high priest: he may not let his hair down, tear his clothes (the standard Israelite mourning gestures), or attend even his parents’ funeral (21:11–12). The provision sets the high priest one degree above ordinary priests, who could mourn close kin (21:1–4). The theological logic: the high priest in the role of mediator must remain ritually pristine, even at the cost of normal human grief. Caiaphas’s tearing his clothes at Jesus’ trial (Matt 26:65, Mark 14:63) is a deliberate violation of this verse — Mark’s wording ("the high priest tore his garments") is exact in its breach of Lev 21:10, and the gospel readers sensitive to Levitical detail would have recognized the procedural irregularity. Hebrews 4:14–15 takes the high priest’s strict separation as background for its argument about Christ as the high priest who is "able to sympathize with our weaknesses" — Christ as high priest specifically does not maintain Levitical separation from suffering. The verse is one of the OT’s most exact specifications of cultic role-discipline.

↩ ◇ Note. The Molech prohibition. Molech (Hebrew Molekh) is the deity of child-sacrifice the OT polemicizes against most consistently — cf. Lev 20:2–5, 1 Kgs 11:7 (Solomon’s Molech high place), 2 Kgs 23:10 (Josiah destroying the Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned), Jer 7:31, 19:5, 32:35. Most modern critical scholarship debates whether Molech was a separate deity, a title (the Hebrew root m-l-k means "king") for various ANE deities, or a specific sacrificial type (so M. Weinfeld read molekh as referring to a kind of votive offering rather than a god). Phoenician-Punic archaeological evidence (the tophet at Carthage and similar sites) confirms that infant sacrifice was a real ANE religious practice through the Iron Age. The Valley of Hinnom (Hebrew Gei Hinnom) became, by the time of the NT, the Hebrew root for "Gehenna" — Jesus’ word for the place of final judgment — precisely because of its association with child sacrifice. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest prohibitions of a real and recurring religious practice in the surrounding cultures, with long theological afterlife in both Jewish and Christian eschatological vocabulary.

↩ ◇ Note. The high priest’s marriage law. The chapter restricts the high priest to marrying only a virgin from his own people — explicitly excluding widows, divorced women, prostitutes, and "defiled" women that ordinary priests could marry (cf. 21:7, where ordinary priests are forbidden only the prostitute and the divorced woman). The provision intensifies the high priest’s ritual separation in personal life: even his marriage must perform the same purity-distinction his sanctuary work performs. The arrangement has long influenced Christian theological reflection on clerical celibacy and ministerial marriage — the medieval Latin church drew on the high priest’s separation to argue for clerical celibacy, while the Eastern church and most Protestant traditions have read the OT distinction as descriptive of an obsolete cultic role rather than prescriptive for Christian ministry. Heb 7:26–28 takes the high priest’s required perfection as background for its argument about Christ’s priestly office — the OT high priest’s rigorously specified separation becomes the foreshadowing the NT writer treats as fulfilled in the resurrected Christ "who has been made perfect forever."

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MULE (Hebrews pered), so called from the quick step of the animal or its power of carrying loads. It is not probable that the Hebrews bred mules, as this was strictly forbidden in the law (Leviticus 19:19), although their use was not forbidden. We find them in common use even by kings and nobles (2 Samuel 18:9; 1 Kings 1:33; 2 Kings 5:17; Psalm 32:9). They are not mentioned, however, till the time of David, for the word rendered “mules” (R.V. correctly, “hot springs”) in Genesis 36:24 (yemim) properly denotes the warm springs of Callirhoe, on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea. In David’s reign they became very common (2 Samuel 13:29; 1 Kings 10:25). Mules are not mentioned in the New Testament. Perhaps they had by that time ceased to be used in Palestine.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEARD The mode of wearing it was definitely prescribed to the Jews (Leviticus 19:27; 21:5). Hence the import of Ezekiel’s (5:1-4) description of the “razor” i.e., the agents of an angry providence being used against the guilty nation of the Jews. It was a part of a Jew’s daily toilet to anoint his beard with oil and perfume (Psalm 133:2). Beards were trimmed with the most fastidious care (2 Samuel 19:24), and their neglet was an indication of deep sorrow (Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 41:5). The custom was to shave or pluck off the hair as a sign of mourning (Isaiah 50:6; Jeremiah 48:37; Ezra 9:3). The beards of David’s ambassadors were cut off by hanun (2 Samuel 10:4) as a mark of indignity. On the other hand, the Egyptians carefully shaved the hair off their faces, and they compelled their slaves to do so also (Genesis 41:14).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BALANCE occurs in Leviticus 19:36 and Isaiah 46:6, as the rendering of the Hebrew kanch’, which properly means “a reed” or “a cane,” then a rod or beam of a balance. This same word is translated “measuring reed” in Ezekiel 40:3,5; 42:16-18. There is another Hebrew word, mozena’yim, i.e., “two poisers”, also so rendered (Daniel 5:27). The balances as represented on the most ancient Egyptian monuments resemble those now in use. A “pair of balances” is a symbol of justice and fair dealing (Job 31:6; Psalm 62:9; Proverbs 11:1). The expression denotes great want and scarcity in Revelation 6:5.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FAST The sole fast required by the law of Moses was that of the great Day of Atonement (q.v.), Leviticus 23:26-32. It is called “the fast” (Acts 27:9). The only other mention of a periodical fast in the Old Testament is in Zechariah 7:1-7; 8:19, from which it appears that during their captivity the Jews observed four annual fasts. (1.) The fast of the fourth month, kept on the seventeenth day of Tammuz, the anniversary of the capture of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans; to commemorate also the incident recorded Exodus 32:19. (Comp. Jeremiah 52:6, 7.) (2.) The fast of the fifth month, kept on the ninth of Ab (comp. Numbers 14:27), to commemorate the burning of the city and temple (Jeremiah 52:12, 13). (3.) The fast of the seventh month, kept on the third of Tisri (comp. 2 Kings 25), the anniversary of the murder of Gedaliah (Jeremiah 41:1, 2). (4.) The fast of the tenth month (comp. Jeremiah 52:4; Ezekiel 33:21; 2 Kings 25:1), to commemorate the beginning of the siege of the holy city by Nebuchadnezzar. There was in addition to these the fast appointed by Esther (4:16). Public national fasts on account of sin or to supplicate divine favour were sometimes held. (1.) 1 Samuel 7:6; (2.) 2 Chronicles 20:3; (3.) Jeremiah 36:6-10; (4.) Nehemiah 9:1. There were also local fasts. (1.) Judges 20:26; (2.) 2 Samuel 1:12; (3.) 1 Samuel 31:13; (4.) 1 Kings 21:9-12; (5.) Ezra 8:21-23: (6.) Jonah 3:5-9. There are many instances of private occasional fasting (1 Samuel 1:7: 20:34; 2 Samuel 3:35; 12:16; 1 Kings 21:27; Ezra 10:6; Nehemiah 1:4; Daniel 10:2,3). Moses fasted forty days (Exodus 24:18; 34:28), and so also did Elijah (1 Kings 19:8). Our Lord fasted forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2). In the lapse of time the practice of fasting was lamentably abused (Isaiah 58:4; Jeremiah 14:12; Zechariah 7:5). Our Lord rebuked the Pharisees for their hypocritical pretences in fasting (Matthew 6:16). He himself appointed no fast. The early Christians, however, observed the ordinary fasts according to the law of their fathers (Acts 13:3; 14:23; 2 Corinthians 6:5).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DAY The Jews reckoned the day from sunset to sunset (Leviticus 23:32). It was originally divided into three parts (Psalm 55:17). “The heat of the day” (1 Samuel 11:11; Nehemiah 7:3) was at our nine o’clock, and “the cool of the day” just before sunset (Genesis 3:8). Before the Captivity the Jews divided the night into three watches, (1) from sunset to midnight (Lamentations 2:19); (2) from midnight till the cock-crowing (Judges 7:19); and (3) from the cock-crowing till sunrise (Exodus 14:24). In the New Testament the division of the Greeks and Romans into four watches was adopted (Mark 13:35). (See WATCHES.) The division of the day by hours is first mentioned in Daniel 3:6, 15; 4:19; 5:5. This mode of reckoning was borrowed from the Chaldeans. The reckoning of twelve hours was from sunrise to sunset, and accordingly the hours were of variable length (John 11:9). The word “day” sometimes signifies an indefinite time (Genesis 2:4; Isaiah 22:5; Hebrews 3:8, etc.). In Job 3:1 it denotes a birthday, and in Isaiah 2:12, Acts 17:31, and 2 Timothy 1:18, the great day of final judgment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TABERNACLES , FEAST OF the third of the great annual festivals of the Jews (Leviticus 23:33-43). It is also called the “feast of ingathering” (Exodus 23:16; Deuteronomy 16:13). It was celebrated immediately after the harvest, in the month Tisri, and the celebration lasted for eight days (Leviticus 23:33-43). During that period the people left their homes and lived in booths formed of the branches of trees. The sacrifices offered at this time are mentioned in Numbers 29:13-38. It was at the time of this feast that Solomon’s temple was dedicated (1 Kings 8:2). Mention is made of it after the return from the Captivity. This feast was designed (1) to be a memorial of the wilderness wanderings, when the people dwelt in booths (Leviticus 23:43), and (2) to be a harvest thanksgiving (Nehemiah 8:9-18). The Jews, at a later time, introduced two appendages to the original festival, viz., (1) that of drawing water from the Pool of Siloam, and pouring it upon the altar (John 7:2, 37), as a memorial of the water from the rock in Horeb; and (2) of lighting the lamps at night, a memorial of the pillar of fire by night during their wanderings. “The feast of Tabernacles, the harvest festival of the Jewish Church, was the most popular and important festival after the Captivity. At Jerusalem it was a gala day. It was to the autumn pilgrims, who arrived on the 14th (of the month Tisri, the feast beginning on the 15th) day, like entrance into a silvan city. Roofs and courtyards, streets and squares, roads and gardens, were green with boughs of citron and myrtle, palm and willow. The booths recalled the pilgrimage through the wilderness. The ingathering of fruits prophesied of the spiritual harvest.”, Valling’s Jesus Christ, p. 133.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GOODLY TREES boughs of, were to be carried in festive procession on the first day of the feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40). This was probably the olive tree (Nehemiah 8:15), although no special tree is mentioned.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WILLOWS (1.) Hebrews ‘arabim (Leviticus 23:40; Job 40:22; Isaiah 15:7; 44:3, 4; Psalm 137:1, 2). This was supposed to be the weeping willow, called by Linnaeus Salix Babylonica, from the reference in Psalm 137. This tree is frequently found “on the coast, overhanging wells and pools. There is a conspicuous tree of this species over a pond in the plain of Acre, and others on the Phoenician plain.” There are several species of the salix in Palestine, but it is not indigenous to Babylonia, nor was it cultivated there. Some are of opinion that the tree intended is the tamarisk or poplar. (2.) Hebrews tzaphtzaphah (Ezekiel 17:5), called by the Arabs the safsaf, the general name for the willow. This may be the Salix AEgyptica of naturalists. Tristram thinks that by the “willow by the water-courses,” the Nerium oleander, the rose-bay oleander, is meant. He says, “It fringes the Upper Jordan, dipping its wavy crown of red into the spray in the rapids under Hermon, and is nutured by the oozy marshes in the Lower Jordan nearly as far as to Jericho...On the Arnon, on the Jabbok, and the Yarmuk it forms a continuous fringe. In many of the streams of Moab it forms a complete screen, which the sun’s rays can never penetrate to evaporate the precious moisture. The wild boar lies safely ensconced under its impervious cover.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KINSMAN Hebrews goel, from root meaning to redeem. The goel among the Hebrews was the nearest male blood relation alive. Certain important obligations devolved upon him toward his next of kin. (1.) If any one from poverty was unable to redeem his inheritance, it was the duty of the kinsman to redeem it (Leviticus 25:25,28; Ruth 3:9, 12). He was also required to redeem his relation who had sold himself into slavery (Leviticus 25:48, 49). God is the Goel of his people because he redeems them (Exodus 6:6; Isaiah 43:1; 41:14; 44:6, 22; 48:20; Psalm 103:4; Job 19:25, etc.). (2.) The goel also was the avenger (q.v.) of blood (Numbers 35:21) in the case of the murder of the next of kin.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ALMS Not found in the Old Testament, but repeatedly in the New. The Mosaic legislation (Leviticus 25:35; Deuteronomy 15:7) tended to promote a spirit of charity, and to prevent the occurrence of destitution among the people. Such passages as these, Psalm 41:1; 112:9; Proverbs 14:31; Isaiah 10:2; Amos 2:7; Jeremiah 5:28; Ezekiel 22:29, would also naturally foster the same benevolent spirit. In the time of our Lord begging was common (Mark 10:46; Acts 3:2). The Pharisees were very ostentatious in their almsgivings (Matthew 6:2). The spirit by which the Christian ought to be actuated in this duty is set forth in 1 John 3:17. A regard to the state of the poor and needy is enjoined as a Christian duty (Luke 3:11; 6:30; Matthew 6:1; Acts 9:36; 10:2, 4), a duty which was not neglected by the early Christians (Luke 14:13; Acts 20:35; Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:25-27; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4). They cared not only for the poor among themselves, but contributed also to the necessities of those at a distance (Acts 11:29; 24:17; 2 Corinthians 9:12). Our Lord and his attendants showed an example also in this (John 13:29). In modern times the “poor-laws” have introduced an element which modifies considerably the form in which we may discharge this Christian duty.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). USURY the sum paid for the use of money, hence interest; not, as in the modern sense, exorbitant interest. The Jews were forbidden to exact usury (Leviticus 25:36, 37), only, however, in their dealings with each other (Deuteronomy 23:19, 20). The violation of this law was viewed as a great crime (Psalm 15:5; Proverbs 28:8; Jeremiah 15:10). After the Return, and later, this law was much neglected (Nehemiah 5:7, 10).

REDEEMER Hebrews goel; i.e., one charged with the duty of restoring the rights of another and avenging his wrongs (Leviticus 25:48, 49; Numbers 5:8; Ruth 4:1; Job 19:25; Psalm 19:14; 78:35, etc.). This title is peculiarly applied to Christ. He redeems us from all evil by the payment of a ransom (q.v.). (See REDEMPTION.)
